To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

in recreational contexts the adolescents bring classroom-related activities outside the classroom, and that by means of interactional and linguistic practices they integrate different cultural frames.
the participants by means of various interactional practices and by use of particular linguistic resources, integrate different cultural and linguistic frames.

the participants by employment and use of various interactional means, including the employment of various non-standard linguistic features integrate different cultural frames, and that this process is part of an ongoing process of re-negotiations between peer-culture, school, and society.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the ways in which the participants in interactional sequences in recreational learning contexts bring together peer-culture and classroom related activities, and how they thereby renegotiate dominant discourses and enregisterments of speech style in contemporary Denmark.

how young people in a late modern context negotiate their identities through their use of language in interaction, as well as with the ways in which the use of particular linguistic resources can be viewed as part of a process of enregisterment of a particular speech style.
the ways in which youth, in interactional settings outside of formal schooling, engage with, challenge and re-negotiate the dominant educational discourse.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the adolescents’ practices are not only re-negotiations, but also re-articulations, of social class relations in contemporary Copenhagen.
the participants in the present data do not seem to be engaged in the same kind of ‘crossing’ as Rampton’s British participants.
the participants’ interactional practices in recreational contexts can be seen to challenge and renegotiate the boundaries between educational discourses and youth peer culture.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

in both contexts, youth engage in practices that challenge dominant discursive assumptions about what is considered appropriate in educational contexts and that they do so by drawing on resources from the peer culture and the school culture.

the adolescents are not just “playing around” with their linguistic resources, but that the interactional and linguistic practices are highly consequential for the adolescents’ positioning in relation to different discourses, and for the adolescents’ construction of social identities.

the adolescents in both contexts are engaged in re-negotiations between educational discourses and peer-culture, however the interactional practices and linguistic resources employed are quite different.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the interactional renegotiations of educational discourses among late modern youth in Copenhagen, as well as in other contexts, are not simply about the integration of different cultural frames, or the bringing together of different cultural repertoires.

the participants’ interactional practices in the two different recreational contexts can be seen as attempts to renegotiate social relations and social identities in the light of the participants’ social class positions and their social class aspirations.

the participants in our study are not simply reproducing the dominant social order, but rather they are engaged in processes of re-negotiation of the boundaries between different cultural frames, and of different discourses.
